title: HLG vs PQ: Two Ways to Encode HDR Video
description: HLG and PQ are two HDR transfer-function systems.
direct: HLG and PQ interpret brightness differently. Check the clip’s transfer function before choosing a color conversion, even if both files are labeled HDR.

cards.choice.heading: Same HDR family, different interpretation
cards.choice.body: The ICC BT.2100 registry identifies both PQ and HLG transfer functions. A .mov or .mp4 extension does not tell you which system the picture uses.
sections.explain.heading: Why switching a label is not conversion
sections.explain.body: HLG is designed around a relative scene-based signal, while PQ describes an absolute display-light relationship. Reading one as the other can produce an incorrect image. Changing a filename, selecting H.264 or attaching a color label does not by itself perform the required transformation. Follow the source interpretation and destination color pipeline.
sections.practice.heading: When an SDR copy is useful
sections.practice.body: For a destination that requests standard Rec.709 SDR, our iPhone app provides HDR-to-SDR conversion with an H.264 MP4 output. Conversion re-encodes the video and changes the highlight presentation; it is not lossless restoration. Its first three conversions are free; further conversions require a purchase. Keep HDR originals for future HDR workflows. No HLG-to-PQ conversion control is claimed.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: If my inspector only says BT.2020, have I identified HLG?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: No. That may identify the color primaries. Look for a separate transfer field or the original recording settings before choosing HLG or PQ.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: Do I need an SDR copy when the recipient already supports HDR?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: If the original opens and displays correctly in the receiving workflow, keep it for HDR delivery. Make an SDR copy separately when another destination requires it.
